lines.text: Not Sri Lanka. Not Pakistan. America: nearly $202 billion from 2000 to 2023, says AidData.
lines.say: Not Sri Lanka. Not Pakistan. America: nearly two hundred two billion dollars from two thousand to twenty twenty-three, says AidData.

lines.say: Most of it went to companies and projects here, not to the US government itself.

lines.text: Worldwide, China's state lenders committed about $2.2 trillion in loans and grants over those years.
lines.say: Worldwide, China's state lenders committed about two point two trillion dollars in loans and grants over those years.

lines.text: And the most famous slice of that money has a name you've probably heard: the Belt and Road.
lines.say: And the most famous slice of that money has a name you've probably heard: the Belt and Road.

lines.text: So how does China lend? Is it a bank, a debt trap, or something in between?
lines.say: So how does China lend? Is it a bank, a debt trap, or something in between?

lines.text: And how do mines and railways in Africa end up inside the battery in your pocket?
lines.say: And how do mines and railways in Africa end up inside the battery in your pocket?

lines.text: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.
lines.say: Quick note: this is news and education, not financial advice.

lines.text: Chapter one: the big idea.
lines.say: Chapter one: the big idea.

lines.text: In September 2013, Xi Jinping proposed a Silk Road Economic Belt, in a speech in Kazakhstan.
lines.say: In September twenty thirteen, Xi Jinping proposed a Silk Road Economic Belt, in a speech in Kazakhstan.

lines.text: A month later, speaking in Indonesia, he added a 21st Century Maritime Silk Road.
lines.say: A month later, speaking in Indonesia, he added a twenty-first century Maritime Silk Road.

lines.text: Here's the confusing part. The belt is the land routes, like railways, roads and pipelines. The road is the sea.
lines.say: Here's the confusing part. The belt is the land routes, like railways, roads and pipelines. The road is the sea.

lines.text: Yes, the road is in the ocean. Naming things is hard.
lines.say: Yes, the road is in the ocean. Naming things is hard.

lines.text: China says more than 150 countries have signed Belt and Road papers, by its own count.
lines.say: China says more than a hundred fifty countries have signed Belt and Road papers, by its own count.

lines.text: AidData, a research lab at William & Mary, spent years piecing together those loan records.
lines.say: AidData, a research lab at William and Mary, spent years piecing together those loan records.

lines.text: Their 2021 report counted 13,427 projects worth $843 billion, in 165 countries.
lines.say: Their twenty twenty-one report counted thirteen thousand four hundred twenty-seven projects worth eight hundred forty-three billion dollars, in a hundred sixty-five countries.

lines.text: In an average Belt and Road year, China spent about $85 billion on overseas development. The US spent about $37 billion.
lines.say: In an average Belt and Road year, China spent about eighty-five billion dollars on overseas development. The US spent about thirty-seven billion.

lines.text: Our math: that's about 2.3 times as much. And most of China's money wasn't gifts. It was loans.
lines.say: Our math: that's about two point three times as much. And most of China's money wasn't gifts. It was loans.

lines.text: So what does a Chinese loan actually look like on paper?
lines.say: So what does a Chinese loan actually look like on paper?

lines.text: Chapter two: how China lends.
lines.say: Chapter two: how China lends.

lines.text: Most of the money comes from two state-owned banks: China Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China.
lines.say: Most of the money comes from two state-owned banks: China Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China.

lines.text: They're not charities. AidData found the average Chinese loan carried an interest rate of 4.2%.
lines.say: They're not charities. AidData found the average Chinese loan carried an interest rate of four point two percent.

lines.text: It was usually repaid in under 10 years, with under two years of breathing room first.
lines.say: It was usually repaid in under ten years, with under two years of breathing room first.

lines.text: By AidData's comparison, a typical aid loan from Germany or Japan ran about 1.1% over 28 years.
lines.say: By AidData's comparison, a typical aid loan from Germany or Japan ran about one point one percent over twenty-eight years.

lines.text: Here's what that gap does. Our math, simplified: a $1 billion loan, repaid in equal yearly payments.
lines.say: Here's what that gap does. Our math, simplified: a one billion dollar loan, repaid in equal yearly payments.

lines.text: At 4.2% over 10 years, the payment is about $124.5 million a year.
lines.say: At four point two percent over ten years, the payment is about a hundred twenty-four and a half million dollars a year.

lines.text: At 1.1% over 28 years, it's about $41.7 million a year. Roughly a third of the bill.
lines.say: At one point one percent over twenty-eight years, it's about forty-one point seven million dollars a year. Roughly a third of the bill.

lines.text: Total interest differs less: about $245 million versus $167 million. The squeeze is speed.
lines.say: Total interest differs less: about two hundred forty-five million versus a hundred sixty-seven million dollars. The squeeze is speed.

lines.text: It's like paying off a house in 10 years at a higher rate instead of 28 at a low one. About triple the yearly bill.
lines.say: It's like paying off a house in ten years at a higher rate instead of twenty-eight at a low one. About triple the yearly bill.

lines.text: Then there's collateral. AidData says lending backed by collateral, guarantees or insurance rose from about 30% in the early 2000s to nearly 60%.
lines.say: Then there's collateral. AidData says lending backed by collateral, guarantees or insurance rose from about thirty percent in the early two thousands to nearly sixty percent.

lines.text: In 2021, researchers read 100 Chinese loan contracts. Every one signed since 2014 had a confidentiality clause.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-one, researchers read a hundred Chinese loan contracts. Every one signed since twenty fourteen had a confidentiality clause.

lines.text: Many also kept the Chinese debt out of group debt deals with other government lenders, known as the Paris Club.
lines.say: Many also kept the Chinese debt out of group debt deals with other government lenders, known as the Paris Club.

lines.text: And much of the money went to state companies and project firms, so it often didn't show up as government debt.
lines.say: And much of the money went to state companies and project firms, so it often didn't show up as government debt.

lines.text: AidData called this hidden debt, and its 2021 report put it at about $385 billion.
lines.say: AidData called this hidden debt, and its twenty twenty-one report put it at about three hundred eighty-five billion dollars.

lines.text: In 42 countries, public debt exposure to China was more than 10% of the whole economy.
lines.say: In forty-two countries, public debt exposure to China was more than ten percent of the whole economy.

lines.text: None of that proves a trap. But it makes the loans pricey, fast and hard to see. Now, real cases.
lines.say: None of that proves a trap. But it makes the loans pricey, fast and hard to see. Now, real cases.

lines.text: Chapter three: three famous cases.
lines.say: Chapter three: three famous cases.

lines.text: Case one: Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, built with loans from China's Export-Import Bank.
lines.say: Case one: Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, built with loans from China's Export-Import Bank.

lines.text: Critics called it a white elephant. In 2017, Sri Lanka leased a 70% stake to a Chinese state firm for 99 years.
lines.say: Critics called it a white elephant. In twenty seventeen, Sri Lanka leased a seventy percent stake to a Chinese state firm for ninety-nine years.

lines.text: The firm, China Merchants Port, paid $1.12 billion. It became the most famous Belt and Road story.
lines.say: The firm, China Merchants Port, paid one point one two billion dollars. It became the most famous Belt and Road story.

lines.text: The headline version: China grabbed a port when Sri Lanka couldn't pay. The researchers' version is messier.
lines.say: The headline version: China grabbed a port when Sri Lanka couldn't pay. The researchers' version is messier.

lines.text: The lease was a separate deal: it didn't cancel the port loans. The cash helped ease a dollar crunch.
lines.say: The lease was a separate deal: it didn't cancel the port loans. The cash helped ease a dollar crunch.

lines.text: When Sri Lanka stopped paying foreign debts in April 2022, China held a tenth to a fifth, depending on the count. Bondholders held more.
lines.say: When Sri Lanka stopped paying foreign debts in April twenty twenty-two, China held a tenth to a fifth, depending on the count. Bondholders held more.

lines.text: So China mattered a lot, but it wasn't the biggest lender in the room.
lines.say: So China mattered a lot, but it wasn't the biggest lender in the room.

lines.text: Case two: Zambia, a big copper producer in southern Africa.
lines.say: Case two: Zambia, a big copper producer in southern Africa.

lines.text: In November 2020, Zambia missed a payment on its international bonds: the first African default of the pandemic era.
lines.say: In November twenty twenty, Zambia missed a payment on its international bonds: the first African default of the pandemic era.

lines.text: China was its biggest government lender, and getting China, France, other governments and bondholders to agree took years.
lines.say: China was its biggest government lender, and getting China, France, other governments and bondholders to agree took years.

lines.text: In June 2023, Zambia struck a $6.3 billion deal with its government lenders. Bondholders followed in 2024.
lines.say: In June twenty twenty-three, Zambia struck a six point three billion dollar deal with its government lenders. Bondholders followed in twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: Case three: Kenya's Standard Gauge Railway, from the port of Mombasa to Nairobi, which opened in 2017.
lines.say: Case three: Kenya's Standard Gauge Railway, from the port of Mombasa to Nairobi, which opened in twenty seventeen.

lines.text: China's Export-Import Bank financed about 90% of it, with roughly $3.2 billion in loans.
lines.say: China's Export-Import Bank financed about ninety percent of it, with roughly three point two billion dollars in loans.

lines.text: Paying in dollars got painful. In October 2025, Kenya switched three of those loans into Chinese yuan.
lines.say: Paying in dollars got painful. In October twenty twenty-five, Kenya switched three of those loans into Chinese yuan.

lines.text: Kenya's Treasury said the rate fell from over 6% to about 3%, saving about $215 million a year.
lines.say: Kenya's Treasury said the rate fell from over six percent to about three percent, saving about two hundred fifteen million dollars a year.

lines.text: Pakistan has its own version: the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a plan reported at about $62 billion by 2018.
lines.say: Pakistan has its own version: the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a plan reported at about sixty-two billion dollars by twenty eighteen.

lines.text: A port, a railway, power plants. Different countries, a similar pattern: a big build, then a hard repayment.
lines.say: A port, a railway, power plants. Different countries, a similar pattern: a big build, then a hard repayment.

lines.text: Chapter four: trap or myth?
lines.say: Chapter four: trap or myth?

lines.text: So is it debt-trap diplomacy? Lend too much, then grab the asset when the country can't pay?
lines.say: So is it debt-trap diplomacy? Lend too much, then grab the asset when the country can't pay?

lines.text: That idea took off after Hambantota. Critics point to short terms, collateral, secrecy and hidden debt.
lines.say: That idea took off after Hambantota. Critics point to short terms, collateral, secrecy and hidden debt.

lines.text: Now the other side. A 2020 Chatham House study found the projects in Sri Lanka and Malaysia were driven mostly by local governments.
lines.say: Now the other side. A twenty twenty Chatham House study found the projects in Sri Lanka and Malaysia were driven mostly by local governments.

lines.text: The Hambantota port, for example, was a long-standing dream of Sri Lanka's ruling Rajapaksa family.
lines.say: The Hambantota port, for example, was a long-standing dream of Sri Lanka's ruling Rajapaksa family.

lines.text: In 2021, researchers Deborah Brautigam and Meg Rithmire wrote that Chinese banks had never actually seized an asset from any country.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-one, researchers Deborah Brautigam and Meg Rithmire wrote that Chinese banks had never actually seized an asset from any country.

lines.text: Rhodium Group studied 40 Chinese debt renegotiations in 2019 and counted just one asset seizure: Sri Lanka's port.
lines.say: Rhodium Group studied forty Chinese debt renegotiations in twenty nineteen and counted just one asset seizure: Sri Lanka's port.

lines.text: So which is it? The evidence points to something less dramatic, but still serious.
lines.say: So which is it? The evidence points to something less dramatic, but still serious.

lines.text: Researchers find little sign of a master plan to seize assets, and plenty of expensive, secretive loans that strained some borrowers.
lines.say: Researchers find little sign of a master plan to seize assets, and plenty of expensive, secretive loans that strained some borrowers.

lines.text: China isn't the only reason poor countries struggle. On the IMF's September 2025 list, about half of low-income countries were at high risk of, or in, debt distress.
lines.say: China isn't the only reason poor countries struggle. On the I M F's September twenty twenty-five list, about half of low-income countries were at high risk of, or in, debt distress.

lines.text: Bondholders, Western banks and big global lenders lent to these countries too.
lines.say: Bondholders, Western banks and big global lenders lent to these countries too.

lines.text: When borrowers got in trouble, China often lent again: $240 billion of rescue lending by the end of 2021, says AidData.
lines.say: When borrowers got in trouble, China often lent again: two hundred forty billion dollars of rescue lending by the end of twenty twenty-one, says AidData.

lines.text: Lending to countries in debt distress went from under 5% of China's overseas lending in 2010 to 60% in 2022.
lines.say: Lending to countries in debt distress went from under five percent of China's overseas lending in twenty ten to sixty percent in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: That's what a lender does when its borrowers are struggling: it lends more just to keep the old loans alive.
lines.say: That's what a lender does when its borrowers are struggling: it lends more just to keep the old loans alive.

lines.text: Which brings us to the twist. By 2023, the Lowy Institute says, 60 developing countries paid China more than they got in new loans.
lines.say: Which brings us to the twist. By twenty twenty-three, the Lowy Institute says, sixty developing countries paid China more than they got in new loans.

lines.text: Chapter five: the flip, and your wallet.
lines.say: Chapter five: the flip, and your wallet.

lines.text: Here's Chinese lending to African governments, from Boston University's latest database, released in November 2025.
lines.say: Here's Chinese lending to African governments, from Boston University's latest database, released in November twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: At the 2016 peak, Chinese lenders committed about $28.8 billion to Africa in a single year.
lines.say: At the twenty sixteen peak, Chinese lenders committed about twenty-eight point eight billion dollars to Africa in a single year.

lines.text: Since 2020, it's stayed under $5 billion a year. In 2023, it was about $3.9 billion.
lines.say: Since twenty twenty, it's stayed under five billion dollars a year. In twenty twenty-three, it was about three point nine billion.

lines.text: By 2024, it had fallen to about $2.1 billion, spread across just six projects.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-four, it had fallen to about two point one billion dollars, spread across just six projects.

lines.text: Our math: that's about 7% of the 2016 peak. The firehose turned into a garden hose.
lines.say: Our math: that's about seven percent of the twenty sixteen peak. The firehose turned into a garden hose.

lines.text: Meanwhile, old loans are coming due. The Lowy Institute estimated developing countries owe China about $35 billion in payments in 2025.
lines.say: Meanwhile, old loans are coming due. The Lowy Institute estimated developing countries owe China about thirty-five billion dollars in payments in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: About $22 billion of it comes from the 75 poorest countries: money that can't go to schools or hospitals.
lines.say: About twenty-two billion dollars of it comes from the seventy-five poorest countries: money that can't go to schools or hospitals.

lines.text: But don't call the Belt and Road dead. It's changing shape.
lines.say: But don't call the Belt and Road dead. It's changing shape.

lines.text: In the first half of 2026, a University of Queensland report counted about $49.8 billion of Chinese investment and $76.5 billion of building contracts there.
lines.say: In the first half of twenty twenty-six, a University of Queensland report counted about forty-nine point eight billion dollars of Chinese investment and seventy-six point five billion of building contracts there.

lines.text: Our math: about $126 billion, a record first half. Those are deals, not loans, led by energy, and nearly half by private firms.
lines.say: Our math: about a hundred twenty-six billion dollars, a record first half. Those are deals, not loans, led by energy, and nearly half by private firms.

lines.text: So how does this reach your wallet? Start with that $202 billion into America, mostly loans to companies.
lines.say: So how does this reach your wallet? Start with that two hundred two billion dollars into America, mostly loans to companies.

lines.text: Next, raw materials. Chinese money helped build mines, railways and ports that move copper and cobalt.
lines.say: Next, raw materials. Chinese money helped build mines, railways and ports that move copper and cobalt.

lines.text: Congo mines roughly seven of every ten tons of the world's cobalt, a key metal in phone and electric car batteries.
lines.say: Congo mines roughly seven of every ten tons of the world's cobalt, a key metal in phone and electric car batteries.

lines.text: In 2024, Congo and its Chinese partners revised a mines-for-roads deal: up to $7 billion for infrastructure, tied to copper prices.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-four, Congo and its Chinese partners revised a mines-for-roads deal, with up to seven billion dollars for infrastructure, tied to copper prices.

lines.text: When deals like that work, or stall, it can ripple into metal prices, and into what your phone, car or shipping costs.
lines.say: When deals like that work, or stall, it can ripple into metal prices, and into what your phone, car or shipping costs.

lines.text: There's also a rival offer. In June 2022, the G7 set a goal to mobilize $600 billion for infrastructure by 2027.
lines.say: There's also a rival offer. In June twenty twenty-two, the G seven set a goal to mobilize six hundred billion dollars for infrastructure by twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: It's called the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment. The US pledged $200 billion of it.
lines.say: It's called the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment. The US pledged two hundred billion dollars of it.

lines.text: Its flagship is the Lobito Corridor, a railway linking Africa's copper belt to an Atlantic port in Angola.
lines.say: Its flagship is the Lobito Corridor, a railway linking Africa's copper belt to an Atlantic port in Angola.

lines.text: Which you prefer is a political call. The money fact: two big camps now compete to finance the world's roads and ports.
lines.say: Which you prefer is a political call. The money fact: two big camps now compete to finance the world's roads and ports.

lines.text: Competition can give borrowers more options, or pile on more debt. The terms decide which.
lines.say: Competition can give borrowers more options, or pile on more debt. The terms decide which.

lines.text: Chapter six: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: One: the Belt and Road began in 2013, and AidData counted $843 billion of projects by 2021.
lines.say: One: the Belt and Road began in twenty thirteen, and AidData counted eight hundred forty-three billion dollars of projects by twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: Two: the loans cost more and were repaid faster than aid loans, often secured and secret.
lines.say: Two: the loans cost more and were repaid faster than aid loans, often secured and secret.

lines.text: Three: Sri Lanka, Zambia and Kenya show real strain, but researchers find little proof of a plan to seize assets.
lines.say: Three: Sri Lanka, Zambia and Kenya show real strain, but researchers find little proof of a plan to seize assets.

lines.text: Four: new lending has shrunk, repayments to China hit an estimated $35 billion in 2025, and investment is taking over.
lines.say: Four: new lending has shrunk, repayments to China hit an estimated thirty-five billion dollars in twenty twenty-five, and investment is taking over.

lines.text: And the biggest single recipient of all that Chinese state money? Not a Belt and Road country. America.
lines.say: And the biggest single recipient of all that Chinese state money? Not a Belt and Road country. America.

lines.text: Like any loan, the terms matter more than the headline. For countries, and for you.
lines.say: Like any loan, the terms matter more than the headline. For countries, and for you.

post.title: China's state lenders sent more money to the US than anywhere else. Here's the Belt and Road.
post.ig: China's state lenders sent about $202 billion to the US from 2000 to 2023. Here's how China lends to the world.
post.tiktok: China's biggest borrower isn't Sri Lanka or Pakistan. It's America. Here's how the Belt and Road really works.
post.yt_desc:
From 2000 to 2023, China's state lenders and donors committed about $2.2 trillion worldwide, and the single biggest recipient was the United States, at nearly $202 billion, according to AidData. This video explains the Belt and Road Initiative: how China's policy banks lend, why a 4.2% loan repaid in under 10 years squeezes a budget (with our worked example), and what really happened in Sri Lanka, Zambia, Kenya and Pakistan. We lay out both sides of the debt-trap debate, show how China went from top lender to top debt collector, and follow the money to your wallet: cobalt in your batteries, Chinese state loans to US companies, and the G7's $600 billion infrastructure plan.

CHAPTERS

Sources: AidData, Chasing China (Nov 2025) and Banking on the Belt and Road (Sept 2021); AidData, Kiel Institute, CGD and PIIE, How China Lends (March 2021); Horn, Parks, Reinhart and Trebesch, China as an International Lender of Last Resort (March 2023); Boston University Global Development Policy Center, Chinese Loans to Africa Database (2000-2024 edition, Nov 2025); Lowy Institute, Peak Repayment (May 2025); Christoph Nedopil, University of Queensland / Green Finance & Development Center, China BRI Investment Report 2026 H1 (July 2026); Chatham House (Aug 2020); The Atlantic (Feb 2021); Rhodium Group, New Data on the Debt Trap Question (2019); IMF LIC debt sustainability list (Sept 30, 2025); The Diplomat (Jan 2020); Reuters (2020-2024); Bloomberg (Oct 2025); USGS; White House PGII fact sheets (2022, 2024).

News and education, not financial advice.
